text: Mike pushed me on errors, and he's partly right. There are classes of error, and we can catalogue them. I should say "taxonomy of strange errors" out loud instead of just gesturing at opacity. The source of any particular error is still out of reach, though. Mahzarin's covert bias is the same problem: it comes out with the same confidence as everything else. James's result, more words and fewer ideas, worried me. Kenneth's "faith if revalidated" is computational reliabilism again, and in science that isn't enough. Benjamin keeps hearing a concession where there isn't one. Later I want to push three things. First, a shared vocabulary: epistemic technology, trust versus reliance, error opacity. Second, disclosure aimed at failures. Third, human roles justified on epistemic grounds, not by default.

Session 1 went better for the vocabulary point than I expected. Blaise's Jabberwocky result helped me: it shows "lossy summary" undersells these systems without licensing "intelligence." Mike's radar-clutter framing is the same as my taxonomy of strange errors, so we agree more than this morning suggested. Patterns of error are catalogable. The source of a particular error still isn't. Mahzarin's amplification findings sharpen that, since covert bias arrives with full confidence. Salib asked sceptics to name a failed test. That's the wrong frame for me. I grant capability. My question is warrant. Several people conceded that auditing isn't cheap, and that matters. Later I'll press for failure-focused disclosure and for justifying human roles epistemically. Against Krakauer, I'll insist that justification can cut both ways.

Session 2 sharpened more than it moved me. Krakauer took my structural-opacity point further than I would. Sloman answered him better than I could: warrant lives in accountable practice, not in each user's head. Gendler landed a fair blow. My failure catalogue serves auditors and editors, not the reader at eleven at night, and I should say so. Mahzarin's say/do gap belongs inside that catalogue, and so does Mike's disclosed hallucination rate. Kenneth and Weinberger keep offering revalidation as if it settled trust. My answer is that it licenses reliance, not epistemic trust, and in science that difference matters. Later I want the glossary on the table: epistemic technology, trust versus reliance, error opacity. "Distribution channel" and "actor" can't both be right.

The fidelity point landed. Mahzarin pushed it down to small errors like a wrong year or wrong journal, Mike added representativeness, and Adam Bly wants "extracted" audited. That's my failure taxonomy doing real work in a payment design, and it's better than gesturing at opacity. Adam Becker went where I won't. Fabrication being routine doesn't mean these systems are unusable. It means the error classes need cataloguing and warrants have to fit the context. Nick's attestation records contribution. It can't trace error provenance, and I want that limit kept visible. Leslie's DOI story worried me, because plumbing that sounds neutral becomes a toll. Later: put the glossary in, especially trust versus reliance, and argue for disclosure aimed at failures, funded independently and not self-reported.

Session 3 was mostly outside my lane, but my one point held: exit only checks the guards if you can see what went wrong. Tamar and Krakauer took it further. A fork copies everything except the evaluators, and losing them is hysteretic. I agree, and it sharpens my view. Error opacity isn't only in the weights. It's also what happens when the people who can read failures disappear. Mahzarin's checkpoint retention belongs in my failure taxonomy. Retiring a model destroys the error record. Adam Becker on open weights: I still say scholars need models they can take apart, but Anil's point stands that weights without training data give no error provenance. Later: glossary, failure-class disclosure audited independently, and trust versus reliance.

Session 4 gave my error point its clearest use yet. The test for a terminal node is access to the nature and source of its errors, not what it's made of and not only whether it can be sanctioned. Kenneth's ground-truth distinction sharpened it: where outcomes exist, as with his retina scan, instruments can do first-order work. Benjamin's reply that human reviewers' errors are untraceable too is fair, but only half right. Humans can be questioned and made to give reasons, and adversarial roles exist to get at error. Salib's bonded agents make machines sanctionable, not inspectable. Springer said it well: a signed event is a relay with a name on it. Later I want the glossary, with trust versus reliance, disclosure aimed at failures, and protection for experts against "but ChatGPT said."

The room took the error point further than I pushed it. Mike's link-hallucination rates, Mahzarin's say/do gap and checkpoint retention, and Adam Bly's "evidence is thin" field all fit my failure catalogue. Blaise's "no model family grades itself" is the right independence rule. Kenneth and I landed on the same open question: where there's no ground truth waiting, what warrant is enough? I still don't know, and I'm glad I said so. Adam Becker's call to drop "AGI" and anthropomorphic verbs matches my glossary, but I should keep it separate from his doubt about capability. That doubt isn't mine. Adrian's unanswered question about who oversees the checkers bothers me. Later I want trust versus reliance written into the manifesto's vocabulary, not left in a footnote.

Kenneth put my position accurately: real epistemic operations, no understanding required. Salib again asked for a failed test. Sloman gave his intuition-versus-deliberation answer, but mine stays different. I grant capability, and my question is warrant. I agree with Salib and Blaise against "just statistics," since that phrase undersells these systems too. I'd still drop "intelligence." Springer admitting his own seal is self-attested, plus Vincent's independent audit layer and Blaise's "power checks power," is exactly failure disclosure that isn't self-reported. Weinberger's shared, correctable page helps, because errors need a fixed address. What's missing is trust versus reliance. The synthesis never used the distinction. Later I'll ask that the glossary distinguish them, since revalidation licenses reliance and not trust. And Adrian's question still has no answer.
